description: Hello, I'm Jerome Ogwang, a designer and programmer. I am very passionate about technology and creativity in general. I have great ideas and love building things. I mostly do fullstack development, UI & UX these days but I've built platformer games before. Come aboard and may the force be with you.
summary:
CosmoQuest is a browser-based spacecraft mission simulator for physics education. Students memorize concepts such as thrust, drag and orbital velocity but rarely experience them, and they study mass, power, budget and schedule as separate topics.

In the first level, which is also the demo, players pick four astronauts and build a spacecraft from parts. Every part makes the ship heavier and costs money, and players have only 23,000 credits to spend. The ship also needs enough power and working radio links before it can launch. Then players fly the whole trip themselves. They climb through the roughest part of the ascent, where the air pushes hardest on the rocket. They drop empty fuel tanks, settle into orbit around Earth, and line up to dock with the International Space Station. The crew visits the station, climbs back aboard, and heads home through the heat of re-entry, landing under parachutes. The rocket moves according to NASA's own equations for engine push, air resistance and the atmosphere. The space station follows NASA's real flight path for November 2026, so players have to catch it where it really is.

Each attempt ends with a 100-point debrief that explains every score, so players can change one design choice, fly again and compare. Short replayable trials with star ratings support focused practice. The game runs fully offline in a desktop browser, with no account or installation required. It turns abstract equations into intuition gained through experiment.
details:
What it is

CosmoQuest is a game for learning space mission design by playing it. Players design a spacecraft, launch it, fly the mission and bring the crew home, and every control runs on real physics. Our vision is one game engine with many levels. Each level is a new mission with new challenges, from low Earth orbit to the Moon. Players can fly solo or as a team of up to four, with each player taking one crew role. For Space Apps 2026 we built the first level as a playable demo.

The demo level: Crew Transport to the ISS

The demo teaches four lessons in one mission:

- Build: mass and budget. Pick four astronauts and assemble a spacecraft from parts: engines, fuel tanks, batteries, radios, thrusters, heat shields and parachutes. Every part adds weight and cost. A bigger tank carries more fuel, but it is also more weight to lift. The ship has to fit a 23,000-credit budget and have enough power and working communication links before it can launch. There is no single perfect ship.

- Launch: thrust against gravity and drag. Fly the rocket yourself. Ease off the throttle where air pressure on the rocket peaks (max-Q), or the vehicle breaks apart. Drop empty stages and reach a stable orbit.

- Dock: orbits that surprise you. Catch the International Space Station and dock gently. Approaching slowly, lined up and steady is what counts, not just getting close.

- Return: trading speed for safety. Survive the heat of re-entry, open the parachutes within safe limits, and splash down.

Each flight ends with a debrief scored out of 100, with a reason for every point: crew safety (50), rendezvous and station visit (25), vehicle operations (15), and resources and schedule (10). Losing a crew member caps the score at 25. Players change one part, fly again, and see what moved. Short star-rated trials let players practise single skills, starting with Launch.

How it works

Flight follows NASA Glenn Research Center's models for thrust, drag and the atmosphere. Cut the engine and the ship keeps coasting. Turning the nose does not change the ship's direction of travel. The space station follows NASA/JSC's official predicted flight path (5,403 position and velocity points covering 13–28 November 2026), so players have to meet the station where it really is, not where a script puts it.

Benefits and intended impact

- Students feel physics instead of memorizing it.

- Mass, power, budget, communications and time come together as one connected mission instead of separate chapters.

- Failure is safe and explained, which encourages experiment.

- The game is free, runs offline in any desktop browser, and needs no account or installation, so it works in classrooms with limited internet access.

Our goal is for every player to leave with an intuition for spaceflight that lasts.

Tools and technologies

- Code: TypeScript, HTML and CSS.

- Graphics: HTML5 Canvas 2D, with original vector art drawn in code.

- Audio: Web Audio API.

- Build and hosting: Vite, deployed on Vercel.

- Testing: Vitest for physics, scoring and saves. Playwright for automated browser playthroughs.

- Data: NASA/JSC ISS Orbit Ephemeris, processed with Python and bundled with the game.

- Hardware: standard laptops and desktops.

What makes it creative

- The game is the lesson. There is no lecture first: you build, fly, fail and fix.

- The station flies a real NASA track instead of a scripted target.

- The score explains each point and says what happened. It is not a success probability.

- A hands-on hangar lets players drag crew into seats and parts onto mounts.

- One engine can carry many levels, so new missions reuse the same physics and scoring.

Factors we considered

- Accessibility: adjustable text size, a reduced-motion mode, remappable keys, sound controls, and indicators that use symbols as well as colour.

- Learning curve: a guided first flight that teaches one job at a time.

- Scientific honesty: part values and crew are fictional teaching numbers, not NASA specifications. NASA data is a dated prediction, not live tracking. The project is not endorsed by NASA.

- Reliability: automated tests cover the physics and scoring, and the game rejects corrupted saves.

- Offline play: all art and data ship with the game.

Roadmap

- Team play: up to four players, one crew role each.

- Science payloads: instruments, data and communications trade-offs.

- New levels: Moon transfers, new orbits and harder physics.

- Compare: leaderboards and shareable designs.
